items.title: NVIDIA SkillSpector scans an agent skill before it is installed; Softanza checks its agent files the same way
items.summary: NVIDIA SkillSpector is an open-source (Apache 2.0) scanner for the skills that coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI install, at v2.13.4 on November 4, 2026. It checks a skill from a directory, a file, a zip, a URL or a Git repository against 71 patterns in 17 categories, among them prompt injection, data exfiltration, excessive agency, memory poisoning and MCP tool poisoning, first by static analysis and optionally by a language model, and reports a 0-100 risk score in terminal, JSON, Markdown or SARIF. Its README cites a study of 31,132 marketplace skills in which 26.1% held at least one vulnerability and 5.2% showed likely malicious intent.

notice.developer: A skill your coding agent installs runs with its trust; scan it first with SkillSpector's static mode, which needs no model and no key.
notice.maintainer: A Softanza agent file is data that may come from a colleague or a model; Softanza checks its text for the same risks SkillSpector names, and Radar shows the scan before any install it suggests.

actions.do: check a .pia agent file at load for the risks SkillSpector names that apply to it (instructions that override the agent's role, endpoints that could carry data out, tools beyond the declared task, MCP servers with broader rights than needed), reported in the unified rule shape through stzRuleReport beside the existing function and posture refusals
show a SkillSpector static scan before every skill install a Radar lesson suggests

items.title: A2UI 1.0: an open protocol for agents to answer with a native screen; Zane gives it intent and law, and a projection to it
items.summary: On November 11, 2026 the A2UI project, started at Google, released A2UI 1.0 under Apache 2.0: a streaming protocol in which an agent sends a screen as data, built only from components the app registered in a locked catalog, and each app draws it with its own native components in React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI and soon Jetpack Compose. Version 1.0 adds typed function calls in both directions, components from several catalogs on one screen, and A2UI Express, which its authors say describes the same screen in about three times fewer output tokens than JSON. Gemini, Atlassian and ByteDance ship it.

notice.developer: An agent can now answer with a form, a chart or a choice that every app draws natively, sent as data and never as code; A2UI 1.0 is the open protocol for it.
notice.maintainer: Zane declares what the human is doing and checks it against its constitution; an A2UI projection lets a checked Zane declaration reach every A2UI renderer, and an A2UI check lets Zane judge screens other agents send.

actions.do: add an A2UI v1.0 projection: compile a checked Zane declaration into createSurface, updateComponents and updateDataModel messages over a Zane catalog, so a screen the constitution passed renders natively in every A2UI renderer
read an A2UI message stream an agent produced and check it against the constitution's structural rules before it renders, citing rule numbers, as the verifier does for .zane files

measure which screen format a small local model writes validly under the engine's constrained decoding: a Zane declaration, A2UI JSON or A2UI Express, counting valid screens and output tokens with Granite-4.0-1b on a fixed set of requests

items.title: Liquid AI's LFM3: six 2B-class models on one backbone, built for the device; Softanza learns from its decision models
items.summary: On October 27, 2026 Liquid AI released LFM3, six open-weight models of about 2 billion parameters each (text, vision with video, audio with speech output, omni, and two d1 decision models), all branched from one 1.7B base. The base mixes 13 gated short-convolution layers with 5 sliding-window and 6 global attention layers, fits in about 1 GB at 4 bits, reads 256K tokens and covers 16 languages, Arabic and French among them. The d1 models answer a list of questions about one input in a single forward pass, each answer with a calibrated probability.

notice.developer: A 1 GB open model for local agents now reads Arabic and French with a 256K context, and its d1 sibling answers several yes/no, choice and score questions about one input in one pass.
notice.maintainer: Softanza already reads answers by probability, which beat generation on its golden sets; it measures LFM3's d1 shape, many questions over one shared prefill, and weighs the LFM3 decoder family beside Gemma 4.

actions.do: measure answering several option questions over one shared prefill of the same input, the shape of LFM3's d1 models, against one StzOptionProbabilities call per question, on the support-desk golden sets: same answers, fewer prefill tokens

weigh the LFM3 decoder family (gated short convolutions, sliding-window and gated global attention, partial RoPE) beside Gemma 4 for the engine's next decoder port, then put LFM3-1.7B before the model court against Granite-4.0-1b with its speeds recorded

sources.title: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

items.title: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B: a 4 GB model for local agents; Softanza adds its Gemma 4 family and takes it to the model court
items.summary: On October 23, 2026 NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B, a small language model post-trained by reinforcement learning from Google's Gemma 4 E4B for multi-turn tool use, instruction following and grounding. It has 8 billion parameters, 4 billion of them effective, a 64K-token context, and ships as a 4 GB Q4_K_M GGUF file for llama.cpp with a companion DFlash drafter for speculative decoding. Its weights, training data and recipes are published under the OpenMDW-1.1 licence, and NVIDIA's own benchmark table puts it ahead of Gemma 4 E4B on most of 21 agent and instruction tests.

notice.developer: A 4 GB open model tuned for tool calls and short answers now runs locally through llama.cpp; Softanza tests it on its own golden sets before it offers it.
notice.maintainer: Bolt E4B uses the Gemma 4 architecture, so Softanza's engine adds that decoder family first, then the model court compares Bolt with Granite-4.0-1b on extraction, classification and brief.

actions.do: add the Gemma 4 decoder family (Gemma 4 E4B and its per-layer embeddings) to the engine's own Zig decoder, checked token by token against a reference run of the same GGUF file

put Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B (Q4_K_M) before the model court as a challenger to Granite-4.0-1b on the support-desk golden sets, read by probability as the incumbent is, and record CPU and wgpu speeds on the 6 GB laptop GPU beside the scores

sources.title: NVIDIA's models on Hugging Face, Nemotron 3.5

items.title: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B finds pages by text or by image in 34 languages; Softanza measures it on Arabic and French retrieval
items.summary: On October 20, 2026 NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B, an embedding model that turns a query, a passage or the image of a document page into one vector, for retrieval across text, tables, charts and infographics. NVIDIA evaluated text retrieval in 34 languages, Arabic, French and Persian among them, and image retrieval in 18; its vectors can be cut to 1024 or 512 dimensions and stay usable once normalised. It is published under OpenMDW-1.1, with an NVFP4 variant for recent NVIDIA GPUs.

notice.developer: A 1B open model now retrieves document pages from their images as well as their text, in many languages; Softanza keeps its own embedding model until a multilingual test says otherwise.
notice.maintainer: Softanza adds Arabic and French retrieval items to its embedding golden set, so the court can judge multilingual challengers such as Nemotron 3.5 Embed against MiniLM and SigLIP2.

actions.do: add Arabic and French items to the retrieval golden set, so the model court can judge a multilingual embedding challenger against all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on text and SigLIP2 on page images

items.title: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Parse reads a page into text, tables and layout with 0.63 billion parameters; Softanza's OCR court hears it
items.summary: On October 17, 2026 NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a 0.631-billion-parameter model that turns a page image into text, tables, chart data, reading order, semantic classes and bounding boxes, exported as Markdown, HTML or JSON. NVIDIA reports 75.20 on the ParseBench benchmark in its three-pass mode, the best of the systems it compares, and multilingual OCR evaluated over 163 language and script entries. On November 4 it added a native 89.3-million-parameter DFlash2 drafter for speculative decoding; the model is published under OpenMDW-1.1.

notice.developer: An open 0.63B model now reads whole pages, tables and charts included, into Markdown or JSON; Softanza measures it against its own OCR pipeline before choosing.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's OCR court measures Nemotron 3.5 Parse on its golden pages, by a reference run, before any port of its encoder and decoder is planned.

actions.do: run Nemotron 3.5 Parse once by its published reference path on the OCR plane's golden pages, single and triple pass, and enter the result in the OCR court beside the PP-OCR pipeline and Granite-Docling, with the languages and scripts each one reads

items.title: NVIDIA OpenShell governs an agent from outside its process; Softanza adds that boundary to the rules it already decides in code
items.summary: NVIDIA OpenShell is an open-source (Apache 2.0) runtime for AI agents, at v0.1.8 on November 10, 2026, and moving to the CNCF. Each agent runs in a sandbox whose files, system calls and network are confined by the kernel, a supervisor outside the agent checks every outbound request against a deny-by-default policy and adds real credentials only to requests bound for approved endpoints, and a prover uses formal logic to show what new access a policy change would grant before it is applied. It runs on Linux, on macOS with Apple Silicon, and on Windows through WSL 2 or Microsoft MXC.

notice.developer: An agent that never holds a real credential cannot leak it: OpenShell adds the secret only to a request bound for an approved endpoint, outside the agent's reach.
notice.maintainer: Softanza already decides in code which functions an agent may call and under which posture; it adds the boundary OpenShell shows, enforcement outside the agent's process, for secrets first and for model-written code next.

actions.do: broker credentials for agents: an agent's outbound call names a secret held in stzSecretStore, and the engine attaches its value only to a request bound for an endpoint the governance approves, so neither the agent's code nor the model ever holds the value

run model-written code and an agent's child processes inside an operating-system boundary outside the agent's process, deny by default on files and network (on Windows a job object or AppContainer, on Linux namespaces with seccomp or Landlock), and measure what each platform enforces natively

show, before a governance change is accepted, the access it adds: the functions, postures, endpoints and secrets an agent could reach after the change and not before, computed from the rules themselves

items.title: NVIDIA Snapshot restores a warmed-up GPU inference worker in seconds; Softanza saves the warm state it pays for, a read prompt
items.summary: On November 8, 2026 NVIDIA released Snapshot v0.3.0, an open-source (Apache 2.0) Kubernetes system that checkpoints a fully initialised GPU inference pod, CPU and GPU memory together, and restores it on another node instead of starting it again. It combines CRIU for the process with NVIDIA's cuda-checkpoint for the GPU, and works with vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. On NVIDIA's own B200 tests, restore was 8.1 to 35.9 times faster than a cold start across 22 configurations, for example 4.7 seconds against 104 seconds for Qwen3-0.6B on vLLM.

notice.developer: Restoring a warm process beats rebuilding it; for a small local model the warm state worth keeping is the prompt the model has already read, which can be saved and reloaded.
notice.maintainer: Softanza loads a small model in 0.2 to 1.3 seconds, so its cost is reading long fixed prompts; it measures saving a prefilled KV cache and restoring it against prefilling again.

actions.do: save the KV cache of a prefilled fixed prompt (system instructions, examples, a document) to disk, keyed by the model's sha256 and the prompt's tokens, and restore it instead of prefilling; measure restore time against the recorded 38.5 tokens per second CPU prefill, and check the next-token probabilities are identical

sources.title: NVIDIA Dynamo Snapshot: Fast Startup for Inference Workloads on Kubernetes

items.title: NVIDIA ships a small drafter with each new model and speeds up llama.cpp; Softanza takes the algorithm into its own decoder
items.summary: On September 3, 2026 NVIDIA said its work with the llama.cpp and vLLM communities gives up to 1.9 times higher local throughput on a GeForce RTX 5090, from GPU kernel work, better speculative decoding and faster prefill. Since then its new models ship with a small DFlash drafter, which llama.cpp's official server runs, and its open-source C++ runtime TensorRT Edge-LLM (0.11.1, October 28) added the Bolt E4B drafter and TensorRT for RTX on Windows. Most of the speed comes from CUDA code for NVIDIA's newest GPUs; the speculative-decoding algorithm itself is portable.

notice.maintainer: Softanza's decoder keeps its CPU and wgpu paths and measures speculative decoding with a small drafter of the same tokenizer, against its recorded 17.6 tokens per second decode.

actions.do: measure speculative decoding in the engine's Zig decoder (a small drafter proposes several tokens, the main model checks them in one pass), with a drafter that shares the main model's tokenizer, against the recorded Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B decode of 17.6 tokens per second on the CPU
record the upstream ggml commit Softanza's vendored copy came from, so each later ggml improvement can be judged against it

sources.title: Sparks Fly: NVIDIA Accelerates Local AI at IFA 2026

items.title: Radar runs for any project: one file says what its agent learns and watches
items.summary: Radar now reads everything that belongs to its project from one file, radar.yaml: the project, the watch, its readers, its map, and what the watching agent learns before each survey. The feed, the site with its trends, and the bar take their names and texts from it, and version 1.1.0 of the bar reads any watch's feed with the key the page gives it.

notice.developer: Any project can run its own Radar: copy the repository, write radar.yaml, and point the bar at your feed with data-feed and data-key.
notice.maintainer: Radar's project-specific values now live in radar.yaml, checked before every run; bar 1.1.0 is the version to pin, and 1.0.0 keeps working.

items.title: A coding agent's "don't ask again" writes secrets into a file that gets published
items.summary: Apiiro reports that when a Claude Code user approves a command with "Yes, and don't ask again", the exact command, including any password or key typed into it, is saved as a permission rule in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project. The file is kept out of git only by the developer's global ignore list, not by the repository's own .gitignore, and Apiiro counted 1,122 public copies on GitHub holding a real secret, out of 104,185.

notice.developer: Open .claude/settings.local.json in each project you use a coding agent in, delete any rule that contains a password, key or token, and rotate it if the file was ever committed.
notice.maintainer: Add .claude/settings.local.json to your repository's own .gitignore, and scan agent folders, transcripts and memory files for passwords written inside commands.

actions.do: add .claude/settings.local.json to the repository's own .gitignore, so the protection travels with the repository and not with one machine
add .claude/settings.local.json to the repository's own .gitignore, for the same reason
add a check for passwords written inside commands (PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p, mysql -p, bearer headers) over agent settings, transcripts, memory files and handoff notes
write the house rule: a secret is referenced as an environment variable in a command, never typed into it

sources.title: Coding Agents Copy Your Secrets to a Hidden File. Thousands Are on GitHub

items.title: Radar's feed is signed: check it came from this repository unchanged
items.summary: Radar publishes an SSH signature beside each feed file, feed/index.json.sig and feed/feed.json.sig, made with one Ed25519 key kept for this purpose by Radar's maintainer. Any reader with OpenSSH can check a feed with ssh-keygen against the public key and the namespace radar-feed. The change adds files and adds nothing to the feed itself, so the feed stays at version 1; docs/FEED.md gives the key, its fingerprint and the command.

notice.developer: Radar's feed carries a signature beside each file; a program that shows its notices should check it with ssh-keygen before showing anything.
notice.maintainer: Pin Radar's key fingerprint in your reader rather than fetching the key from the same place as the feed.

actions.do: add the signature check to the reader proposed in docs/READER.md, with the key's fingerprint pinned in the library

items.title: GitHub will block pull_request_target in public repositories from December 2
items.summary: GitHub announced on November 2, 2026 that from December 2, 2026, GitHub Actions blocks pull_request_target events by default in every public repository unless an Actions event policy allows them. Enforcement is tried in two windows, November 9 and November 16, 16:00 to 18:00 UTC. Private and internal repositories are not affected.

notice.developer: If your public project's workflows use pull_request_target, expect them to fail on November 9 and 16 between 16:00 and 18:00 UTC, and to stop from December 2 unless you allow them.
notice.maintainer: Check your public repositories for pull_request_target before December 2; Softanza's own repositories do not use it.

items.title: Code repaired by a model after an API change can pass its checks and still be wrong
items.summary: A study submitted on November 5, 2026 looks at code that models repair after documented changes in CPython, Node.js and SQLite. Repairs that run cleanly can still give wrong answers: a gate built on typical inputs let 41% of the wrong repairs through, and adding one input written from the release note cut that to 6.5%. The expected outputs came from the old program on the old runtime.

notice.developer: When an agent repairs code for a changed API, test the repair with one input that exercises the change, and take the expected answer from the old version.
notice.learner: A program that runs without errors can still be wrong: test it with the case that changed, not only with the usual ones.
notice.maintainer: Gate every model-made port or repair on edge inputs taken from the change itself, with expected outputs from the old runtime, never from the model's own tests alone.

actions.do: for code ported to Haro by an agent, gate each change on at least one input that exercises the documented difference, with the expected output read off the old runtime

sources.title: Accepted but Wrong: Silent Failures of LLM Code Repairs after API Migrations

items.title: Radar opens: a public watch on AI, read from Softanza's point of view
items.summary: Softanza opened Radar, a public repository that reads developments in AI at their source and judges each one against what Softanza builds. Every entry is written twice in one file, as a page for people and as data for programs, and a feed is generated from the data.

notice.developer: Softanza now keeps a public watch on AI developments: read it on GitHub, or fetch feed/index.json to show its notices in your own tools.
notice.learner: There is now one place that explains, in plain words, what changes in AI mean for what you learn with Softanza.
notice.maintainer: Radar is open: send it the AI developments that touch your project, and expect the tasks it proposes to reach you through Bangalo.

actions.do: run the first weekly survey and publish its digest
propose a command that reads this feed for its user's audience and level

items.title: Two MCP clients let a malicious server obtain a token meant for another server
items.summary: Two advisories published on November 5, 2026 describe the same flaw in two MCP clients, the Go SDK mcp-go before 1.2.1 and the ChatCLI agent before 1.215.2: the client took the resource named in a server's protected resource metadata without checking that it matched the server it had connected to. A malicious MCP server could name another server on the same authorization server, have the user sign in, and replay the token it received.

notice.developer: If you use mcp-go or ChatCLI, update to mcp-go 1.2.1 or ChatCLI 1.215.2, and only sign in to MCP servers you chose yourself.
notice.maintainer: An MCP client must check that the resource a server declares is the server URL it connected to before it asks for a token.

actions.do: record as a requirement for any MCP client Softanza builds: the declared resource is checked against the configured server URL before a token is requested, with a guard that a mismatching server is refused

sources.title: GHSA-h3x9-8c36-m89w: mcp-go OAuth protected resource metadata not validated
GHSA-2gm2-hpg7-78f2: ChatCLI MCP OAuth resource indicator

items.title: SPILLWAY: an agent may act only on targets that came from a trusted, typed field
items.summary: A paper submitted on November 4, 2026 proposes a defence for tool-using agents against prompt injection that does not rely on a model: a call with side effects is admitted only if every target it names that is not in the user's request was returned in a typed identity field, such as an email address or a channel, by a read-only tool. A rule-based sanitizer removes instruction-like text, and a local model reviews only the calls the rule refused. The authors report no successful in-scope attack across twelve benchmark settings.

notice.developer: A strong defence against prompt injection is a plain rule, not a smarter model: let an agent send or pay only to a target that came from the user or from a trusted, typed field.
notice.maintainer: Compare Softanza's tool governance with SPILLWAY's admission rule: where a side effect's target comes from matters as much as which tool is allowed.

actions.do: study whether Softanza's agent governance can check the provenance of a side effect's target, not only the tool's name, and report what it would take

sources.title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection

items.title: A prompt library ran any function a template named: tools must come from a registry
items.summary: The Python prompt library banks, up to version 2.4.2, read a tool's import path from the text of a prompt template and imported and called whatever it named when the model asked for that tool (CVE-2026-61536, high). Whoever could write a template, in a shared registry or a fetched prompt, could run code in the application. Version 2.4.3 resolves tools only from a registry filled at render time.

notice.developer: If your agent resolves a tool from a name or path found in a prompt or a config file, resolve it only against a list of tools you registered in code.
notice.maintainer: Check that every way an agent finds a tool goes through an explicit registry, never through an import or a lookup built from text.

actions.do: check that declarative agents resolve their tools only against tools registered in code, and add a guard that a tool named only in the agent's text is refused

sources.title: GHSA-64vx-6h2c-rjh7: banks CompletionExtension tool import path
The fix: resolve tool callables from an explicit registry

items.title: Zig 0.17.1 fixes the blockers of 0.17.0; Softanza measures the move from 0.15.2
items.summary: Zig 0.17.1 is a bug-fix release that addresses more than 57 issues reported after 0.17.0, chiefly regressions and upgrade blockers; the project says most users who could not move to 0.17.0 should be able to move to 0.17.1. Its news page dates it November 3, 2026 and its download page November 2.

notice.maintainer: Zig 0.17.1 is the first 0.17 release meant to be upgraded to; Softanza builds on 0.15.2 and measures the move on a branch before it plans it.

actions.do: measure what building the engine on Zig 0.17.1 breaks, on a branch, as one capped build, and report the count before planning the move
measure the same for Haro's VM, after stzlib's measurement and never at the same time
